title: Introduction to C# and .NET
objectives: Explain the purpose of C# and its relationship to .NET.
Identify using, class, Main, statements and code blocks.
Write and run a simple C# console program in an authorized development environment.
introduction: Learn C# uses; .NET runtime; console applications; namespace; class; Main; statements; semicolons; blocks; comments through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
C# is a statically typed language for console, web, desktop and other application development. A .NET SDK builds the program; the runtime executes compiled managed code. using imports namespace names rather than pasting a library into the program. Program is a class, Main is the entry point, braces delimit blocks and semicolons terminate many statements. This course uses an explicit Program/Main structure so beginners can see the entry point; modern top-level statements are an alternative, not required. Console.WriteLine prints a line.
Topics and syntax to practice: C# uses; .NET runtime; console applications; namespace; class; Main; statements; semicolons; blocks; comments
csharp_project_guide: Use your own supported .NET SDK console project (prefer .NET 10 LTS). Check dotnet --list-sdks; create a C# console project, replace Program.cs, and build/run it in your authorized development environment. CodeLab only contacts a separately verified isolated provider when configured; no compiler is currently connected. Ordinary console examples use only the base class library. Database examples additionally require Microsoft.Data.Sqlite in the practice project. Keep files and database inside a dedicated disposable directory; never use CodeLab resources or credentials.
guided_practice:
1. Create a dedicated practice project; inspect the example and its expected effects.
2. Trace the statements and identify data types, control flow, and output before running.
3. Use the documented sample input (stdin one value per line). Compile in your own authorized SDK environment or the verified isolated service when available.
4. Test normal, empty, malformed and boundary inputs; record actual compiler/runtime messages.
5. Complete the independent activity with original source; save it and restricted project/evidence links.

title: Variables, Constants, and Data Types
objectives: Explain declaration using the example.
Implement Variables, Constants, and Data Types in an appropriate practice environment.
Validate normal and boundary inputs and document results.
introduction: Learn declaration; assignment/reassignment; var; const; naming; int/long/double/decimal/char/bool/string; casts; Convert; Parse; TryParse through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Variables store typed values and can be reassigned; const values are fixed at compile time. var infers a compile-time local type from an initializer and is not dynamically typed. Use meaningful camelCase locals and PascalCase type/method names. int and long represent whole numbers; double uses binary floating point; decimal uses decimal arithmetic and needs the m suffix. char is one UTF-16 code unit, bool is true/false, and string is text. Explicit casts can narrow a value and lose information; Convert and Parse may throw on invalid or overflowing input. TryParse reports failure without using exceptions for ordinary invalid numeric input. Always validate the range after parsing.
Topics and syntax to practice: declaration; assignment/reassignment; var; const; naming; int/long/double/decimal/char/bool/string; casts; Convert; Parse; TryParse

title: Input, Output, and Operators
objectives: Explain write/writeline/readline using the example.

introduction: Learn Write/WriteLine/ReadLine; null handling; concatenation/interpolation; arithmetic; comparisons; &&/||/!; assignment; ++/--; precedence through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
ReadLine returns text or null at end of stdin. Write does not add a newline; WriteLine does. Prefer TryParse with an explicit culture and validate the domain. Decimal arithmetic is useful for this calculator; integer division otherwise truncates toward zero. % is remainder. == compares equality while = assigns. && and || short-circuit, which lets the right side be skipped safely. Parentheses make precedence explicit. Compound assignment and increment/decrement update values; avoid overly clever expressions that hide those side effects.

introduction: Learn if/else/else if; nested conditions; switch/expression; ternary; for/while/do/foreach; break/continue; nested loops; counters/accumulators through fictional student data and C# practice.

Conditions select behavior and loops repeat bounded work. Classify continuous ranges, including decimal grades: 90–100 Excellent, 85 to below 90 Very Good, 80 to below 85 Good, 75 to below 80 Passed, otherwise Failed. Validate 0–100 first. foreach visits elements, for is useful for indices, while checks before a body and do checks after it. break ends a loop and continue skips the rest of the current iteration. Counters count records and accumulators total values. Nested loops multiply work; keep limits small and make progress toward termination.

title: Arrays and Methods
objectives: Explain declaration/initialization using the example.
Implement Arrays and Methods in an appropriate practice environment.
Validate normal and boundary inputs and document results.
introduction: Learn declaration/initialization; zero-based indices; updates; Length; foreach; multidimensional arrays; parameters/arguments; returns; void; overloading; scope through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Arrays have fixed length and zero-based indices. new decimal[3] has valid indices 0, 1 and 2. A rectangular array uses a comma between indices and GetLength for each dimension; a jagged array contains arrays. Methods group behavior; parameters declare inputs while arguments supply values. void returns no value; a return statement supplies a result to the caller. Overloading uses different parameter lists, not return type alone. Local scope limits visibility. Validate empty arrays before averages/minimum/maximum. The example uses LINQ for brevity; implement loops yourself to practice accumulators and extrema.
Topics and syntax to practice: declaration/initialization; zero-based indices; updates; Length; foreach; multidimensional arrays; parameters/arguments; returns; void; overloading; scope

explanation:
Strings are immutable: transformations return new strings. Trim removes outer whitespace, not internal spaces. Check length before Substring; use ordinal comparisons for identifiers and choose cultural comparisons deliberately for display/search. Split is useful for simple delimited practice text but is not a complete quoted-CSV parser. List<T> is a mutable generic collection; Count gives its current size. Remove removes a matching value and returns whether it existed; RemoveAt takes an index and needs bounds checks. Do not mutate a List while enumerating it with foreach.

A class describes state and behavior and an object is an instance. Prefer properties for a public contract; private fields store internal state. title: Encapsulation and Inheritance
objectives: Explain public/private/protected/internal using the example.

introduction: Learn public/private/protected/internal; fields; validated properties; getters/setters; base/derived classes; colon syntax; base; protected members; overriding through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Encapsulation protects invariants by controlling state changes. public exposes the contract, private limits a member to its declaring type, protected allows access from derived types, and internal limits access to the assembly. Inheritance models an is-a relationship and C# allows one direct base class. : names the base, base calls its constructor or accesses its member, and virtual/override permit runtime specialization. Prefer composition when reuse does not describe an is-a relationship. Expose read-only views and validated operations rather than mutable internals.

introduction: Learn virtual/override; runtime dispatch; abstract types/methods; interface contracts; multiple interfaces through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Polymorphism lets a base/interface reference invoke the concrete implementation. A virtual base member can be overridden; abstract members require implementation in non-abstract derived classes. explanation:
Choose collections by behavior: Dictionary maps keys, HashSet models uniqueness, Queue is FIFO and Stack is LIFO. LINQ transforms sequences through filtering, sorting, projection, grouping and aggregation. Most sequence pipelines defer enumeration; ToList snapshots results. Guard empty sequences before Average or use an explicit no-data result. FirstOrDefault selects at most the first match while SingleOrDefault asserts at most one and throws for duplicates. introduction: Learn generic classes/methods; type parameters/constraints; Action/Func/Predicate; event/EventArgs; publisher/subscriber through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Generics provide reusable compile-time type-safe components. Constraints state required type capabilities. Action returns void, Func returns a value and Predicate returns bool. A delegate represents compatible callable behavior. Events expose controlled subscription; only the publisher normally raises its declared event. EventArgs carries event data and EventHandler<T> is a conventional pattern. Unsubscribe long-lived handlers to avoid retaining objects. title: Asynchronous Programming
objectives: Explain sync/async using the example.
Implement Asynchronous Programming in an appropriate practice environment.
Validate normal and boundary inputs and document results.
introduction: Learn sync/async; Task/Task<T>; async/await; exceptions; CancellationToken/Source; I/O vs CPU; avoid Result/Wait through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
async methods can suspend at await without blocking their calling thread during a genuinely asynchronous operation; async is not automatically a new thread. Task<T> represents a future result. Use async Task for operations and await exceptions in try/catch; reserve async void for framework event handlers. Cancellation is cooperative: pass the token and honor it. Avoid .Result/.Wait where blocking can deadlock or waste threads. File.ReadAllTextAsync is suitable I/O practice; Task.Delay is a simulation, not a claim of database I/O. CPU-bound work has different scheduling needs; do not wrap every I/O method in Task.Run.
Topics and syntax to practice: sync/async; Task/Task<T>; async/await; exceptions; CancellationToken/Source; I/O vs CPU; avoid Result/Wait

objectives: Explain separation of concerns using the example.

introduction: Learn separation of concerns; UI/services/data/models; repository; MVC; DI; interfaces; configuration; validation; SQL injection; secrets; password hashing; roles; least privilege; logging; disposal; cancellation; nullable references through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Separate UI input/output, service rules and data access; a repository is one possible boundary, not mandatory for every small application. MVC separates model, view and controller responsibilities; dependency injection supplies dependencies rather than hiding them in globals. Nullable reference annotations help catch null risks at build time but are not runtime authorization. Validate at service boundaries, parameterize SQL and enforce roles for every protected operation. Use a supported password-hashing mechanism with individual salts; never plaintext or fast unsalted hashes. Keep secrets out of source, logs and submissions and use a suitable configuration/secret provider; environment variables are not automatically a secure vault. Log sanitized events and dispose/cancel resources reliably.

introduction: Learn authentication/logout/roles; dashboard; student CRUD; reports; OOP/interfaces; LINQ; async; isolated SQLite; architecture; security through fictional student data and C# practice.
explanation:
Build a learner-owned console application as the baseline; desktop or ASP.NET Core is an optional external mode. The fixed PBKDF2 parameters demonstrate salted slow hashing; a real deployment should use a supported identity/password hasher with versioned parameters, rate limits across sessions and a reviewed current policy. The reference login attempts bound a single process, not a production distributed rate limit. Students must refactor it into focused Models/UI/Services/Data, add a viewer provisioning workflow under admin authorization, extend course/recent-student reports, LINQ in service reports and appropriate async file/report loading with cancellation. Microsoft.Data.Sqlite queries remain synchronous. Password input here is for private local practice; do not save credential-bearing stdin in CodeLab. For a web option use ASP.NET Core Identity/authorization and HTTPS, not this console login as a web auth system.
